title: The Date object: one number, many getters
objectives: Explain a `Date` as one number (milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00Z) and read `toISOString()` as that instant printed in UTC
Build dates with the constructor forms, remembering that months are 0-indexed (`new Date(2026, 0, 31)` is January 31)
Tell `getDate` (day of the month) from `getDay` (day of the week, 0–6) when reading a date's parts
Predict how setters mutate in place and overflow: `setMonth` on January 31 lands in March, `setDate(0)` is the previous month's last day
Detect an Invalid Date with `Number.isNaN(d.getTime())`, and know where it fails quietly (`JSON.stringify` writes `null`) and loudly (`toISOString` throws)

questions.prompt: What does a `Date` object actually hold?

options.text: Separate year, month, day and time fields, plus the time zone it was created in
The string it was created from, re-parsed on every `get…` call
A local wall-clock time, which `toISOString()` converts to UTC

questions.explanation: A `Date` wraps a single time value: milliseconds since the epoch, which is defined in UTC. There are no stored fields and no stored zone: `getFullYear()`, `getHours()` and friends compute their answer from that number each time, using the time zone of the machine that's asking. That's why the same `Date` can show different hours on two machines while `getTime()` is identical on both.

options.text: Invalid Date: the month must be written `"02"`

questions.explanation: The month argument is an index from 0 (January) to 11 (December), so `1` is February. The day is not an index: it runs 1–31. Reading `1` as January is the classic off-by-one; the fix when printing is `getMonth() + 1`.

questions.prompt: A task due Tuesday, April 14, 2026 renders as "Due on the 2nd". Which call is in the template?
questions.explanation: `getDay()` is the day of the **week**, 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday); Tuesday is `2`. The day of the **month** is `getDate()`, which would print 14. `getMonth()` is 3 for April (0-indexed). `getUTCDate()` is the day of the month read in UTC, a question for the next unit: 14 or a neighbouring day depending on the time and the machine's zone, never 2.

questions.prompt: `a` and `b` were each built with `new Date(2026, 2, 10)`. Which expression is `true`?
questions.explanation: Two `Date` objects are two objects, and `===`, `==` and `Object.is` all compare object identity, so all three are `false` even though both hold the same instant. Compare the numbers instead. (`<`, `>` and `-` do convert both sides to numbers, which is why `a <= b` is `true` while `a === b` is not.)

questions.prompt: On a laptop in New York (UTC−5 in January), what does `new Date(2026, 0, 1).toISOString()` print?
questions.explanation: The multi-argument constructor builds **local** midnight, which in New York is 05:00 UTC. `toISOString()` always prints UTC, marked by the `Z`, never the machine's offset. `"2025-12-31T19:00"` subtracts the offset in the wrong direction. Run the same line in Tokyo and you get `"2025-12-31T15:00:00.000Z"`: local midnight there is 15:00 UTC the day before.

options.text: `nextWeek` is a number (the new timestamp), and `due` itself moved a week
Nothing: `setDate` returns a new `Date` and leaves `due` alone
Past the end of the month, `setDate` throws a `RangeError`

questions.explanation: Every `Date` setter changes the object in place and returns the new time value as a number. So `due` no longer means "due", and `nextWeek.getDate()` would throw because numbers have no `getDate`. Overflow is not an error: day 38 of March rolls into April. Copy first: `const next = new Date(due); next.setDate(next.getDate() + 7);`.

questions.prompt: The rule is "same day next month, or the last day of a shorter month" (January 31 → February 28, 2026). Which code does that for **every** start date?
questions.explanation: Parking on the 1st means changing the month can't overflow; clamping afterwards applies the rule. Plain `setMonth` keeps day 31, and February 31 rolls into March 3. Adding 30 days assumes every month is 30 days long (January 31 + 30 days is March 2). `setDate(0)` after `setMonth` looks clever because it fixes January 31, but for January 15 it goes to February 15 and then back to January 31.

questions.prompt: `const d = new Date(input);` Which check rejects an Invalid Date?
questions.explanation: An Invalid Date is still a `Date` object (so `instanceof` passes) and objects are truthy (so `!d` passes). The constructor never throws for bad input; it returns a Date whose time value is `NaN`. Checking that number is the only reliable test.

prompts.explanation: Months are indexed 0–11, so December is `11`. Passing `12` would roll over into January 25, 2027.

prompts.prompt: Day 0 of a month is the last day of the month before. Get the number of days in February 2028.
prompts.explanation: Month index `2` is March; day `0` borrows one day back, landing on the last day of February. 2028 is a leap year, so `getDate()` is 29. The same idiom, `new Date(year, month + 1, 0)`, gives the last day of any month.

prompts.prompt: Add a week without moving the caller's `start`.
prompts.explanation: `new Date(start.getTime())` makes an independent copy holding the same instant (plain `new Date(start)` does too). Then the setter changes only the copy. `setDate` handles the month end: March 28 + 7 is April 4.

prompts.prompt: Fail at the boundary instead of passing an Invalid Date along.
code: if (Number.___(due.___())) throw new RangeError(`not a date: ${input}`);
prompts.explanation: An Invalid Date's time value is `NaN`, and `Number.isNaN` is the check that doesn't coerce. Throwing here keeps the failure next to its cause, instead of a `null` in a JSON payload or a `RangeError` from `toISOString()` three calls later.

snippets.question: What's logged? (Any time zone: every value here is local.)
snippets.explanation: `setMonth(1)` keeps the day number, asking for February 31, 2026. February has 28 days that year, so the extra 3 days roll into March: March 3. In 2028, a leap year, it's March 2. The rule you probably wanted (clamp to February 28) has to be written explicitly.

snippets.question: What's logged?
snippets.explanation: Setters return the new timestamp, a number, and change the Date they were called on. So `next` is not a Date at all, and `start` is now March 11. Code that expects `start` to still be the start, or calls `next.getDate()`, breaks.

code: console.log(due instanceof Date, due.getTime(), JSON.stringify({ due }));
snippets.question: What's logged?
snippets.explanation: Month 13 can't be parsed, but the constructor doesn't throw: it returns a real `Date` whose time value is `NaN`. `instanceof` is still `true`. `JSON.stringify` calls `toJSON()`, which returns `null` for an invalid date, so the API receives `"due": null` with no error anywhere. Only `toISOString()` would have thrown.
